title: LINQ and Comprehensions
oneLiner: Querying collections: LINQ's Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy, Any, All and First next to list, dict and set comprehensions and generator expressions, with deferred execution and a side-by-side table.
keyTakeaway: xs.Where(x => x > 0).Select(x => x * 2) is [x * 2 for x in xs if x > 0]. LINQ queries and Python generator expressions are lazy: nothing runs until something reads the results. A LINQ query runs again every time you read it and a generator can be read only once, so call ToList() or list() when you need the results more than once.
explanation:
Most code that works with collections does a few things over and over: keep some items, transform each one, sort, group, add up, or ask whether any or all of them match. Writing a loop each time works, but says how rather than what. Both languages have a compact way to say what.

In C# it's LINQ: methods like Where (keep the items that pass a test), Select (turn each item into something else), OrderBy, GroupBy, Sum and Any, each taking a lambda and chained one after another. They work on any sequence: arrays, lists, dictionaries, and even database tables through libraries like Entity Framework.

Python's equivalent is the comprehension, [expression for item in items if condition], with curly-brace versions that build dicts and sets, plus built-ins like sum, any, all, min, max and sorted. A generator expression, the same thing in round brackets, produces items one at a time instead of building a list.

Both rely on lazy evaluation, which C# calls deferred execution: a query describes the work, and the work happens only when something reads the results. That saves work and memory, but has two consequences worth knowing by heart, both shown in the lesson: a LINQ query runs again each time it's read, and a Python generator is empty the second time.
